column4: This ayah places Mary in labor pains at a palm trunk. It is a distinct Quranic childbirth scene that gives bodily force to the section's dictionary detail for difficult birth; this verse itself centers the labor.
The next ayah tells Mary not to grieve and mentions a stream below her. Its own contribution is relief and provision immediately after the labor scene in 19:23.
This ayah tells Mary to shake the palm trunk so ripe dates fall to her. It continues 19:23's childbirth scene with food provided to the mother after labor, joining burden to gift.
This ayah tells Mary to eat, drink, and be comforted after the birth scene. It completes the immediate care sequence following labor, a specific continuation of the section's birth image.

This ayah restricts displaying women's adornment and names husbands among those to whom it may be shown. It parallels the section's dictionary image of a bride adorned and shown to her husband, while adding a boundary around who may see.

This ayah requires visitors to the Prophet's wives to speak from behind a screen. The link is specifically visibility in a marital setting: it sets a privacy boundary alongside the section's dictionary image of a bride displayed to her husband; the two customs are not identical.

This ayah states that God intends ease rather than hardship in the Ramadan fast. Its own setting is fasting, the same passage as 2:187's permitted nighttime intimacy, and it reuses the section's ease/difficulty pairing in a context independent of a child's sex.

This ayah rebukes the claim that God chose sons for the people while taking female angels for Himself. Its own subject is angelic attribution rather than human birth, but the self-serving male/female valuation directly echoes the section's rejected preference for sons.

This ayah asks whether daughters are assigned to God and sons to the people. It repeats the gendered allocation challenged in 16:57 and directly parallels the section's account of preferring male birth.

This ayah asks whether the people witnessed the creation of angels as female, completing 37:149's challenge to their male/female allocation. It adds the question of who could know or witness that sex assignment.

This ayah asks whether God selected daughters over sons, crystallizing the allocation questioned in 37:149 and the intervening passage. It directly exposes the same gender hierarchy that the section says God's giving dissolves.

This ayah says God does not waste the work of any worker, male or female, and that they are from one another. Its context rewards faithfulness under persecution; the link is the section's shift from sex as a birth measure to conduct and devotion as the measure.

This ayah promises a good life and reward for whoever acts rightly, male or female, while believing. It makes the section's displacement of gendered worth by faithful action explicit in another context.

This ayah promises entry to the Garden to believing men or women who do right, with no injustice to them. It is a further direct statement that moral standing does not follow the male/female distinction at the center of the section.
